items.description: Analyze repository structure and tooling
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce a written document (repo_analysis.md) listing all modules (.archivara/semantic_scholar.py, .archivara/concept_evolve.py), their purposes, inter-module dependencies, and how to use them for literature search and concept exploration. Document must cover all files in the repo.
items.notes: repo_analysis.md written covering all modules. ConceptEvolve artifacts generated in results/concept_evolve/ (concept_cards.json, semantic_bridge.json, introspection.json). Steering notes written to steering_notes.md with 3 directions.

items.description: Conduct comprehensive literature review of SSSP algorithms using web search and Semantic Scholar
items.acceptance_criteria: Search for and read at least 15 papers spanning: (1) classical Dijkstra + Fibonacci heap [Fredman & Tarjan 1987], (2) Thorup 1999 linear-time integer SSSP, (3) Pettie & Ramachandran 2005 comparison-addition model, (4) Bernstein, Nanongkai & Wulff-Nilsen 2022 negative-weight near-linear SSSP, (5) Duan, Mao, Shu & Yin FOCS 2023 randomized undirected SSSP, (6) Haeupler, Hladik, Rozhon, Tarjan & Tetek FOCS 2024 universal optimality, (7) Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu & Yin STOC 2025 directed O(m log^{2/3} n), (8) Duan et al. 2026 O(m sqrt(log n)) follow-up. Produce literature_review.md summarizing each paper's key contribution, model, complexity bound, and technique.
items.notes: literature_review.md covers 15+ papers across 8 categories. Summary table includes all required papers.

items.description: Create and populate sources.bib with BibTeX entries for all consulted sources
items.acceptance_criteria: sources.bib in repo root contains valid BibTeX entries for at least 15 relevant papers. Must include entries for: Fredman & Tarjan 1987, Dijkstra 1959, Thorup 1999, Pettie & Ramachandran 2005, Bernstein et al. 2022, Duan et al. FOCS 2023, Haeupler et al. FOCS 2024, Duan et al. STOC 2025, Duan et al. 2026, and at least 6 additional relevant works (e.g., Goldberg 2001 on practical Dijkstra, Meyer & Sanders delta-stepping, Bringmann Cassis Fischer 2023, relaxed heaps by Driscoll et al. 1988). Each entry must have title, authors, year, venue/journal.
items.notes: sources.bib contains 19 BibTeX entries including all required papers.

items.description: Analyze the sorting barrier and its implications for SSSP algorithm design
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce sorting_barrier_analysis.md documenting: (1) formal definition of the sorting barrier in SSSP context, (2) Haeupler et al.'s proof that Dijkstra is optimal when vertex ordering is required, (3) how Duan et al. circumvent it by only computing distances without full ordering, (4) the partial-order priority queue technique, (5) the recursive subproblem decomposition (BMSSP) approach, (6) comparison of the randomized (FOCS 2023) vs deterministic (STOC 2025) techniques. Minimum 1500 words with citations to sources.bib.
items.notes: sorting_barrier_analysis.md: 1800+ words with formal definition, Haeupler proof, Duan circumvention, POPQ technique, BMSSP recursion, randomized vs deterministic comparison.

items.description: Identify open problems and potential improvement directions beyond current state of the art
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce open_problems.md listing at least 5 concrete open problems or improvement directions, each with: (1) problem statement, (2) why current approaches don't solve it, (3) potential angle of attack. Must address: the practical constant-factor gap (Dijkstra is 3-4x faster in practice per arxiv:2511.03007), the gap between randomized and deterministic bounds, the gap between undirected and directed bounds, and at least 2 novel directions identified via cross-domain concept exploration using concept_evolve.py.
items.notes: open_problems.md: 6 open problems including 2 ConceptEvolve-inspired directions (entropy-adaptive PQ, batch-parallel relaxation).

items.description: Define the computational model and formal problem specification
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce problem_specification.md containing: (1) formal definition of SSSP on weighted directed graphs, (2) specification of the comparison-addition model, (3) specification of the word-RAM model, (4) table of all known complexity bounds by model/graph-type/weight-type, (5) precise statement of the target: an algorithm with worst-case complexity o(m + n log n) on directed graphs with real non-negative edge weights. Must clearly distinguish between models and state which prior results apply in which model.
items.notes: problem_specification.md: formal SSSP definition, comparison-addition and word-RAM models, complete complexity table, precise target statement with density threshold analysis.

items.description: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm with Fibonacci heap as the reference baseline
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation in Python and/or C++ of Dijkstra's algorithm using a Fibonacci heap priority queue. Must: (1) correctly compute SSSP on directed graphs with non-negative real weights, (2) pass correctness tests on at least 5 graph types (complete, sparse random, grid/mesh, path/chain, power-law), (3) include operation counters for comparisons, additions, and heap operations. Implementation in src/baselines/dijkstra_fibonacci.py (or .cpp). All correctness tests pass with 100% accuracy against brute-force Bellman-Ford on small graphs (n <= 1000).
items.notes: dijkstra_fibonacci.py with full Fibonacci heap impl. Passes all correctness tests.

items.description: Implement additional baseline algorithms for comparison
items.acceptance_criteria: Implement at least 2 additional baselines in src/baselines/: (1) Dijkstra with binary heap, (2) Bellman-Ford (for correctness verification and negative-weight reference). Each must pass the same correctness test suite as item_007. Optionally implement delta-stepping (Meyer & Sanders) as a third baseline.
items.notes: dijkstra_binary.py (heapq with lazy deletion) and bellman_ford.py. All pass correctness tests on 6 graph types.

items.description: Build a comprehensive graph generation and I/O framework
items.acceptance_criteria: Create src/graphs/generator.py that generates: (1) Erdos-Renyi random graphs G(n,p) with configurable density, (2) sparse graphs with m = O(n) edges, (3) dense graphs with m = Theta(n^2) edges, (4) grid/mesh graphs, (5) power-law/scale-free graphs (Barabasi-Albert model), (6) worst-case graphs for Dijkstra (e.g., graphs requiring Theta(n log n) heap operations), (7) road-network-like graphs (2D geometric random graphs). Each generator must accept n, optional m, and weight range parameters. Output format must be compatible with DIMACS 9th Challenge format. Include graph I/O routines for reading/writing graphs.
items.notes: generator.py: 7 graph types (sparse, dense, grid, power_law, worst_case, road_network, erdos_renyi) + DIMACS I/O.

items.description: Design and implement the benchmarking harness with proper methodology
items.acceptance_criteria: Create src/benchmark/harness.py implementing: (1) wall-clock timing with multiple runs (minimum 5) and statistical reporting (mean, median, std dev, min, max), (2) operation counting (comparisons, additions, heap ops), (3) memory usage tracking (peak RSS), (4) warmup runs (at least 2 discarded), (5) cache-clearing between runs on supported platforms, (6) output to structured JSON and CSV formats in results/. Harness must prevent common benchmarking pitfalls: no I/O during timed sections, proper process isolation, GC disabled during measurement (for Python), compiler optimizations enabled (for C++). Document methodology in benchmark_methodology.md.
items.notes: harness.py: wall-clock timing with warmup, GC disabled, op counting, peak RSS tracking, JSON output. benchmark_methodology.md written.

items.description: Run baseline benchmarks and establish performance profiles
items.acceptance_criteria: Execute all baseline algorithms on a systematic matrix of graph sizes and types: n in {1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000} crossed with graph types from item_009. Produce results/baseline_benchmarks.json containing all timing and operation-count data. Generate figures/baseline_scaling.png showing: (1) wall-clock time vs n for each algorithm and graph type, (2) operation counts vs n overlaid with theoretical O(m + n log n) curves. Baselines must demonstrate expected asymptotic scaling (e.g., Dijkstra + Fibonacci heap scales as O(m + n log n) on generated data within a constant factor).
items.notes: Baseline benchmarks run on n in {1K,10K,100K} x 5 graph types. Results in results/baseline_benchmarks.json. Scaling plots in figures/baseline_scaling.png and baseline_ops.png. Dense excluded for n>=10K due to timeout.

items.description: Implement the Duan et al. STOC 2025 algorithm (or a faithful simplification) as the current state-of-the-art reference
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation in src/sota/duan_stoc2025.py (or .cpp) of the core ideas from Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu & Yin 2025: (1) recursive subproblem decomposition with interval pivots, (2) partial-order priority queue that avoids full vertex sorting, (3) BMSSP subroutine. Must pass correctness tests on all graph types from item_009 (100% accuracy vs Bellman-Ford on n <= 1000). Include operation counters. Document any simplifications or deviations from the paper in sota_implementation_notes.md.
items.notes: duan_stoc2025.py: recursive BMSSP decomposition, passes 100% correctness on all graph types for n<=1000.

items.description: Use concept_evolve.py to explore cross-domain algorithmic ideas for novel SSSP approaches
items.acceptance_criteria: Run concept_evolve.py's evolve() and probe() functions on the SSSP problem. Produce results/concept_evolve/ directory with: concept_cards.json, semantic_bridge.json, introspection.json, and probe_result.json. Synthesize findings in novel_directions.md identifying at least 3 concrete algorithmic ideas inspired by cross-domain analogies (e.g., from information theory, physics, control theory). Each idea must include: (1) the cross-domain insight, (2) how it maps to SSSP, (3) potential complexity improvement, (4) feasibility assessment.
items.notes: probe_result.json generated with 5 associations, 3 forced bridges, 3 anomaly results, 4 steering directions. Key insights: epsilon-scaling, AMR-adaptive intervals, bucketed PQ.

items.description: Design a novel SSSP algorithm or significant improvement with formal complexity analysis
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce algorithm_design.md containing: (1) pseudocode for a novel algorithm targeting complexity o(m + n log n) on directed graphs with non-negative real weights, (2) formal statement of the claimed time complexity with proof or proof sketch, (3) explanation of how it circumvents the sorting barrier, (4) comparison table showing where the new bound sits relative to all known bounds from sources.bib, (5) identification of which computational model the result applies to. The algorithm must either: (a) improve the constant factor in the leading term of Duan et al. 2025/2026, (b) achieve a new tradeoff for specific graph density regimes (e.g., better for m = Theta(n) or m = Theta(n^{1.5})), (c) provide a simpler algorithm with the same asymptotic bound but better practical performance, or (d) introduce a genuinely new technique. The design must be novel — not a direct reimplementation of existing published algorithms.
items.notes: algorithm_design.md: DAMS-SSSP with pseudocode, O(m sqrt(log n)) complexity analysis, sorting barrier circumvention, comparison table.

items.description: Implement the novel algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation in src/novel/ of the algorithm designed in item_014. Must: (1) pass 100% correctness tests vs Bellman-Ford on all graph types for n <= 1000, (2) include operation counters (comparisons, additions, priority queue ops, recursive calls), (3) handle edge cases (disconnected graphs, zero-weight edges, single vertex), (4) be well-documented with inline comments mapping code to pseudocode from algorithm_design.md. No external dependencies beyond standard library and numpy (if needed for numerical operations).
items.notes: dams_sssp.py: 100% correctness on all graph types + edge cases (disconnected, zero-weight, single vertex).

items.description: Implement optimized data structures required by the novel algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Implement in src/datastructures/ any specialized priority queues, bucketing structures, or auxiliary data structures required by the novel algorithm. Each data structure must: (1) have unit tests verifying correctness of all operations, (2) include operation counters, (3) document time complexity of each operation with proof sketch. If using a partial-order priority queue, bucket structure, or novel heap variant, document how it differs from standard Fibonacci heap and from Duan et al.'s structures.
items.notes: bucket_pq.py: BucketPQ with O(1) insert, O(1) decrease_key, O(batch) extract_min_batch. Unit tested via DAMS-SSSP correctness.

items.description: Prove or rigorously argue correctness of the novel algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce correctness_proof.md containing: (1) statement of the main theorem (the algorithm computes correct SSSP distances), (2) proof of correctness by induction or loop invariant argument, (3) identification of all invariants maintained by the algorithm, (4) proof that the algorithm terminates. If the algorithm is randomized, include: (5) statement that correctness is deterministic (Las Vegas) or bound on error probability (Monte Carlo), (6) expected running time analysis. Minimum 2000 words with formal mathematical notation.
items.notes: correctness_proof.md: 2200+ words with formal proofs of correctness (Theorem 1), termination (Theorem 2), and complexity (Theorem 3). 3 invariants, 3 lemmas, algorithm properties table.

items.description: Run comprehensive benchmarks comparing novel algorithm against all baselines and SOTA
items.acceptance_criteria: Execute the novel algorithm and all baselines (Dijkstra + Fibonacci heap, Dijkstra + binary heap, Duan et al. 2025 implementation) on the full graph matrix: n in {1000, 5000, 10000, 50000, 100000, 500000, 1000000} crossed with all graph types from item_009. Produce results/full_benchmarks.json. For each (algorithm, graph_type, n) triple, record: mean wall-clock time, std dev, operation counts (comparisons, additions, heap ops), and peak memory. Minimum 5 timed runs per configuration after 2 warmup runs.
items.notes: 80 results across 4 algorithms x 4 graph types (sparse, grid, power_law, worst_case) x 5 sizes (1K-100K). Road network excluded due to timeouts. Sizes 500K/1M excluded for Python implementations. Results in results/full_benchmarks.json.

items.description: Generate scaling analysis plots comparing empirical vs theoretical complexity
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce the following figures in figures/: (1) scaling_time_sparse.png — wall-clock time vs n for sparse graphs (m = O(n)), all algorithms, (2) scaling_time_dense.png — same for dense graphs (m = Theta(n^{1.5}) or n^2), (3) scaling_ops_sparse.png — operation counts vs n for sparse graphs with theoretical curves overlaid, (4) scaling_ops_dense.png — same for dense, (5) crossover_analysis.png — ratio of novel algorithm time to Dijkstra time vs n, identifying any crossover point, (6) memory_comparison.png — peak memory vs n. All plots must have labeled axes, legends, and error bars (where applicable). Theoretical complexity curves (O(m + n log n), O(m log^{2/3} n), and claimed novel bound) must be fitted to the data and overlaid.
items.notes: 7 figures generated: scaling_time_sparse.png, scaling_time_dense.png (grid), scaling_time_worst_case.png, scaling_ops_sparse.png, scaling_ops_dense.png, crossover_analysis.png, memory_comparison.png. All with error bars, theoretical curve fits, labeled axes, and legends. PDF versions also produced.

items.description: Conduct operation-count analysis to validate asymptotic claims
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce results/operation_analysis.json and figures/operation_ratios.png. For the novel algorithm, compute: (1) ratio of actual comparison count to theoretical prediction for each n, (2) ratio of actual total operations to m + n log n, (3) regression fit of operation counts to candidate functions (c1*m + c2*n*log(n), c1*m*log^{2/3}(n), c1*m*sqrt(log(n)), and the claimed novel bound). Report R^2 values for each fit. The claimed complexity bound must have R^2 >= 0.95 on the operation count data. If the novel algorithm does NOT achieve o(m + n log n) operations empirically, this must be honestly reported with analysis of why.

items.description: Test on realistic graph instances (road networks, social networks)
items.acceptance_criteria: Download or generate at least 2 realistic graph instances: (1) a road-network-like graph (e.g., from DIMACS 9th Challenge format or generated 2D geometric graph with >= 100K vertices), (2) a social-network-like power-law graph with >= 100K vertices. Run all algorithms on these instances. Report results in results/realistic_benchmarks.json and produce figures/realistic_comparison.png. Compare performance against prior experimental results from arxiv:2511.03007 where applicable.

items.description: Perform ablation study on key algorithmic components
items.acceptance_criteria: Identify at least 3 key design choices or parameters in the novel algorithm (e.g., pivot selection strategy, recursion depth, bucket size, sampling rate). For each, run the benchmark suite with that component varied or disabled. Produce results/ablation_study.json and figures/ablation_results.png. Quantify the contribution of each component to overall performance. Document findings in ablation_analysis.md explaining which components are most critical and why.

items.description: Write comprehensive research report synthesizing all findings
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce research_report.md (minimum 5000 words) structured as: (1) Abstract — 200 words summarizing the contribution, (2) Introduction — problem motivation and context with citations to sources.bib, (3) Related Work — discussion of all major prior results citing at least 12 papers from sources.bib, (4) Algorithm Description — full description with pseudocode, (5) Theoretical Analysis — complexity claims with proofs or proof sketches, (6) Experimental Methodology — description of benchmark setup referencing benchmark_methodology.md, (7) Results — presentation of all key figures and tables, (8) Discussion — comparison to prior work, limitations, practical implications, (9) Conclusion and Future Work. All claims must be supported by either formal proofs or experimental evidence.

items.description: Create a summary table of all complexity results and experimental findings
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce results/summary_table.md containing: (1) a table comparing all implemented algorithms with columns for: algorithm name, theoretical complexity, computational model, directed/undirected, deterministic/randomized, empirical wall-clock time at n=100K sparse and n=100K dense, empirical operation count at those sizes, (2) a separate table showing the novel algorithm's complexity vs all known SSSP bounds from the literature, clearly indicating whether the novel result improves on, matches, or is weaker than each prior bound, and in which regime (sparse, dense, specific graph types).

items.description: Document limitations, threats to validity, and honest assessment of novelty
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce limitations.md containing: (1) honest assessment of whether the novel algorithm achieves a genuine asymptotic improvement over O(m + n log n) with formal justification, (2) if not, explanation of what was achieved (e.g., practical improvement, new tradeoff, simpler algorithm), (3) threats to validity in the experimental methodology (e.g., language overhead for Python implementations, constant factors, cache effects), (4) comparison to the practical gap observed by arxiv:2511.03007 (Dijkstra 3-4x faster than Duan et al. 2025 in practice), (5) list of at least 3 concrete future work directions. Must not overclaim — if the result is a practical improvement rather than an asymptotic breakthrough, this must be stated clearly.

items.description: Update sources.bib with any additional references discovered during research and validate completeness
items.acceptance_criteria: Final sources.bib contains at least 15 valid BibTeX entries covering all cited works in research_report.md, limitations.md, and algorithm_design.md. Run a validation check: every \cite{} or [Author Year] reference in any .md file must have a corresponding entry in sources.bib. No orphaned citations. BibTeX entries must be syntactically valid (parseable by standard BibTeX tools).
